subject: ESS HL
title: Aster River Basin: Water Security and River Basin Management
summary: A fictional river basin used to investigate water security, competing water demands, pollution, stakeholder perspectives and sustainable river-basin management. All names and numerical data are hypothetical and created for examination practice.

resources.title: Resource 1: Basin background
resources.text: The Aster River rises in a forested upland, flows through an irrigated farming district and the city of Meridia, and then enters the internationally protected Luma Wetland. A reservoir upstream of Meridia supplies drinking water, irrigation water and hydropower. During the dry season, low river flow increases competition among users. The regional government is considering a new water-allocation plan that would cap irrigation withdrawals, expand wastewater treatment, introduce seasonal water pricing and guarantee a minimum environmental flow to the wetland.

resources.title: Resource 2: Annual freshwater withdrawals
resources.description: Hypothetical annual freshwater withdrawals in the Aster River Basin.
columns: 2032 projected withdrawal without new policy (million m³)
resources.note: Current long-term renewable freshwater availability is estimated at 760 million m³ per year.

resources.title: Resource 3: Mean monthly river discharge
resources.description: Mean monthly discharge measured downstream of Meridia in a representative year.
resources.note: Ecologists recommend that discharge should not fall below 30 m³ s⁻¹ for prolonged periods if wetland habitat quality is to be maintained.

resources.title: Resource 4: Water-quality survey
resources.description: Hypothetical mean water-quality measurements at three sampling sites.
resources.note: Higher BOD indicates greater oxygen demand by microorganisms decomposing biodegradable organic matter.

resources.title: Resource 5: Stakeholder positions
resources.text: Farmers argue that restricting irrigation could reduce crop yields and rural employment. Meridia's water utility supports higher dry-season prices because it expects demand management to postpone costly supply expansion. Wetland conservation groups support a legally guaranteed environmental flow and stronger nutrient controls. Some low-income urban residents oppose higher household water prices unless a basic water allowance is protected. The national government must also comply with a regional agreement requiring participating jurisdictions to avoid causing significant downstream environmental harm.

subject: ESS HL
title: Verdantia Forest Frontier: Biodiversity, Land Use and Food Production
summary: A fictional tropical forest frontier used to investigate habitat loss, biodiversity decline, agricultural expansion, soil degradation, conservation and sustainable food production. All names and numerical data are hypothetical and created for examination practice.

resources.title: Resource 1: Landscape background
resources.text: The fictional Verdantia Forest Frontier covers 100,000 hectares of lowland tropical landscape. During the last two decades, road construction and export-oriented soybean production have expanded into native forest. The remaining forest contains several endemic bird and amphibian species and provides water regulation, soil protection, carbon storage and pollination services. The government is considering a land-use strategy that would prohibit further clearance in high-biodiversity forest, establish an 8,000-hectare wildlife corridor between two protected areas, charge a levy on high fertilizer use and pay farmers who convert part of their land to agroforestry.

resources.title: Resource 2: Land-use change in Verdantia
resources.description: Hypothetical land-use areas in 2005 and 2025. The total landscape area is 100,000 ha in both years.
resources.note: Most new soybean fields and roads were established in areas that were native forest in 2005.

resources.title: Resource 3: Forest-specialist bird population index
resources.description: A hypothetical index based on repeated surveys of forest-specialist birds. The index is set to 100 in 2005.
resources.note: Survey methods were kept consistent between years. The index represents relative abundance rather than the number of species.

resources.title: Resource 4: Comparison of farming systems
resources.description: Hypothetical mean values from farms with similar rainfall and soil parent material.
resources.note: Yield values are not directly equivalent in market value because the systems produce different combinations of products.

resources.title: Resource 5: Stakeholder positions
resources.text: An agribusiness association argues that soybean expansion provides export earnings, tax revenue and employment and warns that strict land limits could reduce investment. Conservation organizations support the corridor and a permanent ban on clearing high-biodiversity forest because fragmented populations may become isolated. A smallholder cooperative supports payments for agroforestry but opposes rules that could remove productive land without compensation. Indigenous communities downstream emphasize the cultural value of intact forest and clean water. The government states that its goal is to maintain food production while preventing further biodiversity loss and soil degradation.

subject: ESS HL
title: Kestrel Republic: Energy Transition, Climate Policy and Urban Air Quality
summary: A fictional national energy transition used to investigate fossil-fuel dependence, renewable energy, greenhouse-gas mitigation, urban air pollution, energy security and social equity. All names and numerical data are hypothetical and created for examination practice.

resources.title: Resource 1: National energy background
resources.text: The fictional Kestrel Republic has historically generated most of its electricity from domestic coal and imported natural gas. Coal mining provides employment in two inland provinces, while the capital, Aurum City, experiences frequent winter air-pollution episodes. The government has proposed a 2035 energy-transition plan that would retire the oldest coal plants, expand solar and wind generation, add grid-scale storage, introduce a carbon price, strengthen power-station air-pollution controls and provide retraining and income support for workers in coal-dependent communities. A protected basic electricity tariff would remain available for low-income households.

resources.title: Resource 2: Electricity generation mix
resources.description: Hypothetical annual electricity generation in 2025 and under the government's 2035 plan.
resources.note: The plan assumes total electricity demand rises because of economic growth and electrification of transport and heating.

resources.title: Resource 3: Operational emissions from electricity sources
resources.description: Hypothetical average operational emissions. Values exclude construction, fuel extraction and other life-cycle emissions.
resources.note: Zero values indicate no direct operational combustion emissions; they do not imply zero life-cycle environmental impact.

resources.title: Resource 4: Annual mean PM2.5 concentration in Aurum City
resources.description: Hypothetical citywide annual mean PM2.5 concentration under the government's transition scenario.
resources.note: The national policy target is to reduce the annual mean below 25 µg m⁻³ by 2035. Transport, industry and household fuels also contribute to Aurum City's PM2.5, so changes cannot be attributed to the electricity sector alone.

resources.title: Resource 5: Stakeholder positions
resources.text: Coal-worker unions support cleaner air but argue that plant closures should occur only after credible replacement jobs and income protection are available. Renewable-energy companies support faster auctions for solar, wind and storage. Energy-intensive manufacturers worry that carbon pricing could raise electricity costs and reduce international competitiveness. Public-health organizations support rapid coal retirement because lower particulate and sulfur emissions could reduce respiratory and cardiovascular disease. Climate groups argue that the transition should be faster because electricity-sector decarbonization can also support low-carbon transport and heating. The government argues that domestic renewable generation will reduce dependence on imported gas and improve long-term energy security.
